newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Court ruling opens new round in Serbia protests.
newsitem.headline: Court ruling opens new round in Serbia protests.

text.p: Serbia's top court handed control of Belgrade city council to the ruling Socialists amid nationwide protest against alleged poll fraud, but election authorities said the decision would be appealed.

Three weeks of unrest led by the the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition that has challenged the rule of President Slobodan Milosevic, and legal wrangles over the November 17 local election results, appeared set to continue.

Opposition officials said a surprise announcement by the city election commission of appeals against the Serbian Supreme Court ruling might mean Milosevic, facing Western demands to honour democracy, could stage a complete re-run of the elections.

More than 100,000 demonstrators, accusing the Supreme Court of bowing to political pressure and demanding Milosevic's ouster, moved through central Belgrade on Sunday, the 19th day of increasingly angry street protests.
The unprecedented wave of demonstrations against the reversal of the initial opposition victories in the municipal elections has swept across Serbia.
In the southern industrial city of Nis, up to 50,000 people jammed the central square, smashing a television set in protest against biased coverage by state-run media.
In the northern city of Novi Sad, some 10,000 university students staged a protest and vowed to go on strike on Monday to demand recognition of the election results and objective media coverage.
But state television once again blasted the demonstrations in Sunday's main evening news bulletin, accusing the opposition of trying to destabilise the country and deceiving the public.
"This is obviously a major farce aimed at the foreign media and a transparent deception of the citizens," it said. "(Zajedno's) objective is to destabilize Serbia."

Opposition leaders cried foul at the Supreme Court's decision to reverse the initial outcome of the elections and give the Socialists and their allies 66 seats in the 110-member Belgrade assembly, claiming the judicial system was tainted by political bias.
"It is now clear to both the foreign and domestic public that what the Supreme Court did last night was founded on politics, not law," Zajedno lawyer Goran Draganic said.
Five of the 36 Supreme Court judges had earlier protested against the authorities' involvement of the judiciary in the settlement of a political conflict.

While the opposition promised to carry on with protests which have drawn up to 150,000 people a day in Belgrade, there was heightened concern Milosevic might resort to force in a re-run of events in 1991, when tanks were used to suppress the last major challenge to Socialist rule.
Zajedno leader Vuk Draskovic told reporters: "I am expecting tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, that Milosevic will use police, maybe even the army, but we will not stop."
He accused Milosevic of ordering the Supreme Court to reject Zajedno appeals for the return of Belgrade city council seats it won.

Police forces have so far kept a low profile in Belgrade and other Serbian cities, but independent media reported several arrests and claimed some of those detained had been severely beaten while in custody.
Zajedno leaders are concerned that police provocateurs among the marchers could foment trouble and give Milosevic an excuse to turn loose his riot police and quell the protests.
